ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Dwight D. Eisenhower — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Primary care visit to establish care after myocardial infarction and plan a return to full-time work

text.paragraph: Primary care visit to establish care after myocardial infarction and plan a return to full-time work [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: Wants to return to a demanding full-time job and travel without bringing on another heart attack. [S]
Worries that limits on work, golf, and travel will be permanent. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Dwight D. Eisenhower was born on October 14, 1890, in Denison, Texas, to David Jacob and Ida Elizabeth (Stover) Eisenhower. [D]
During his war years Eisenhower smoked about four packs of cigarettes a day; he quit, essentially cold turkey, around 1949 at a doctor's suggestion. [D]

On September 23, 1955, during a working vacation in Denver, Eisenhower played golf at Cherry Hills; chest pain woke him early on September 24, an electrocardiogram taken by a cardiac specialist from Fitzsimons Army Hospital confirmed a heart attack, and he was admitted to Fitzsimons that day. [D]

The electrocardiogram recorded an anterolateral acute myocardial infarction with ST-segment elevation. During the golf game he had complained of what he took to be indigestion, and he was hospitalized more than 24 hours after his symptoms began. [D]
Eisenhower remained at Fitzsimons Army Hospital from September 24 until his discharge on November 11, 1955. [D]

text.paragraph: 4 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

tr.td: Heart attack in Denver after a day of golf: anterolateral myocardial infarction with ST elevation, hospitalized more than 24 hours after symptoms began, then seven weeks at Fitzsimons Army Hospital

Coronary artery disease, single-vessel, after stenting; no angina: active, confirmed [S]

Essential hypertension: active, confirmed [S]
Former heavy cigarette smoker, quit about seven years before intake: active, confirmed [S]

Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin 81 mg and ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily for twelve months after the infarction, then aspirin alone. Guideline: 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for the Management of Patients With Acute Coronary Syndromes (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, acute myocardial infarction, ischemic heart disease, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension monographs (2026) [S]

High-intensity atorvastatin with ezetimibe added for LDL cholesterol above 55 mg/dL; recheck lipids 4 to 12 weeks after the change, then every 3 to 12 months. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (2023); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, acute myocardial infarction, ischemic heart disease, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension monographs (2026) [S]

Metoprolol succinate and lisinopril for blood pressure below 130/80; basic metabolic panel 1 to 2 weeks after an ACE inhibitor change, then every 6 months; reassess the beta-blocker at one year. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (2023); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, acute myocardial infarction, ischemic heart disease, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension monographs (2026) [S]

Cardiology consultation to establish local cardiology care, reassess left ventricular function, and advise on return to full-time work and on the duration of antiplatelet and beta-blocker therapy. Guideline: 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for the Management of Patients With Acute Coronary Syndromes (2025); 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (2023) [S]

After cardiac rehabilitation, a home maintenance program of brisk walking and golf, a Mediterranean-style diet, staying tobacco free, PHQ-2 depression screening at visits, and a written chest-pain plan with sublingual nitroglycerin. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (2023); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, acute myocardial infarction, ischemic heart disease, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension monographs (2026) [S]

Yearly influenza vaccine, pneumococcal vaccine, RSV vaccine, and current COVID-19 vaccine. Guideline: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (2023); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, acute myocardial infarction, ischemic heart disease, hyperlipidemia, and hypertension monographs (2026) [S]
